![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14153452/assets/01902836fd1e91ac829f67a279103a9b3d5732d7b058f03c695b6733a42e673d.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
question.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14153452/assets/c058465d6ca7855446711ebc44f6b23913ee786d2fd9bb32ae6c671964e1ad32.png)

 

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=1$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & ={x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+1\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+x{y}^{2}+x]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}+\frac{5}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{5}{4}y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{19}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}+z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-({x}^{3}+{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}-({x}^{3}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =-{∬}_{D}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{7}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{19}{12}+(-\frac{7}{12}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
